summary: Play the classics that moved the medium forward and pin down the specific techniques that made each one feel ahead of its time (shading, named enemies, enemy tables the player can push back, weapon recoil, smooth frame rates) so you can reuse them on purpose, and watch out for the costs that came with them: punishing power-up loss, longer sessions and display lag.
takeaways: Let a destroyable target rewind the enemy table to ease difficulty
Add recoil animation and tight explosions to make firing feel strong
Low frame rates and display lag drain a game's feel
Remap awkward legacy controls; teach complex inputs with training
Losing every power-up on death makes players want to quit

principles.principle: Let players push difficulty back through an enemy table they influence
principles.why: Xevious has no AI reading your skill; its predefined enemy tables advance as you play, and destroying the radar-station enemy sends you back earlier in the table, making the game easier.
principles.how: Drive spawns from an ordered table that advances with progress or skill, and add one recognizable target that rewinds it when destroyed.
principles.example: Xevious — the radar-station-like enemy rewinds the enemy table
principles.quote: Defeating one brings you back earlier in the enemy table, making the game easier.

principles.principle: Add recoil animation to weapons every time they fire
principles.why: Sakurai singles out Star Force's missile recoil, where the side cannons pull back on every shot, along with its beautiful 5-frame explosion, as details that make the shooting feel great.
principles.how: On each shot, snap the gun or cannon back for a few frames and return it; author explosions as short, deliberate frame sequences.
principles.example: Star Force — side cannons pull back with each missile; 5-frame explosion
principles.quote: Whenever you fire missiles, you get this bam, bam, bam kind of recoil animation.

principles.principle: Protect frame rate and display latency; they carry the game's feel
principles.why: The NES Ghosts 'n Goblins kept every element in place but lost its smoothness and creepiness to a low frame rate, and modern TVs' image processing added enough lag to throw off Sakurai's shots.
principles.how: Budget frame rate first when porting or downscaling, and playtest and record on a low-latency display with image processing off.
principles.anti_pattern: Accepting a faithful but choppy port, or testing on a laggy TV.
principles.example: Ghosts 'n Goblins arcade vs. NES; switching to the low-lag 'Mr. Sakurai Presents' monitor mid-session
principles.quote: Today's monitors and TVs do a great deal of image processing.

principles.principle: Don't strip every power-up on death in a power-up-driven game
principles.why: In games with extreme power-ups like Gradius, losing everything after one death is no fun and makes players want to quit.
principles.how: When a death costs the player their build, check whether they can still realistically recover from that point; if not, soften the loss.
principles.anti_pattern: Resetting all power-ups so a late-game death leaves the player hopelessly underpowered.
principles.example: Gradius — reaching a late area with only a Double cannon after losing power-ups
principles.quote: It's no fun when you lose a life and all your power-ups reset.

summary: Borrow the tools classic arcade games used to welcome and balance players (a no-penalty "trial time", difficulty and resource settings that work as handicaps, clear attack tells), and check that your co-op mode doesn't make two players worse off than one.
takeaways: A no-penalty trial period lets newcomers learn before real stakes
Use difficulty and resource settings as handicaps between unequal players
Co-op can be harder than solo if resources aren't rescaled
Give attacks visual tells; don't rely on audio alone
games: The Genji and the Heike Clans

principles.principle: Offer a no-penalty trial period so newcomers can learn first
principles.why: Space Harrier's 'trial time' let players die as much as they wanted for a while; many arcades kept it on for customers, and Sakurai turned it on to give Arino a fair start.
principles.how: Add an opening window or optional mode where deaths cost nothing, then switch to normal rules.
principles.example: Space Harrier — 'trial time'
principles.quote: It means that during that time, you can die as much as you want.

principles.principle: Use difficulty and resource settings as handicaps between unequal players
principles.why: With no lives setting in The Genji and the Heike Clans, Sakurai took the hardest difficulty and fewest candles and gave Arino the easiest difficulty and most candles, making the contest fair.
principles.how: Expose difficulty and resources (lives, health, enemy aggression) as separate per-player settings so a stronger player can handicap themselves.
principles.example: The Genji and the Heike Clans — hardest/fewest candles vs. easiest/most candles
principles.quote: There was no way to set the number of lives, so I put myself at the hardest difficulty with the lowest number of candles.

principles.principle: Check that co-op doesn't make the game harder than solo
principles.why: In two-player Darius the ships get in each other's way and power-ups only cover one ship, which actually makes it harder; Contra's two-player scroll point sits far forward, which makes it tough.
principles.how: Playtest co-op for shared power-ups budgeted for one player, players blocking each other, and a camera or scroll point that strands the trailing player.
principles.anti_pattern: Dropping a second player into single-player resource and camera tuning unchanged.
principles.example: Darius two-player power-ups; arcade Contra two-player scroll point
principles.quote: The two ships get in each other's way, and you only get enough power-ups for one ship— which actually makes it harder.

principles.principle: Telegraph dangerous attacks with clear visual tells players can react to
principles.why: Punch-Out!! signals your chance to dodge when the opponent's eyes turn yellow, while a player who couldn't hear the audio had no idea when Space Harrier's enemies were firing.
principles.how: Give each major enemy attack a visible cue (a color change, a pose) and don't make sound the only warning.
principles.anti_pattern: Signaling incoming attacks through audio alone.
principles.example: Punch-Out!! — yellow eyes signal the moment to dodge
principles.quote: If the opponent's eyes turn yellow, that's your chance to dodge.

summary: Don't settle creative decisions by majority vote. Give them to the person who holds the big picture, and make sure that person has all the information they need to decide well.
takeaways: Creative decisions belong to whoever holds the big picture
Majority votes produce the safest, most mediocre ideas
Unpopular ideas in planning often become fun once built
Share all problems and solutions so the director decides well
Brighter extremities make character movement easier to read

principles.principle: Let the person with the big picture decide, not a majority vote
principles.why: In creative work more votes don't mean a better answer; majority choices end up the safest and most mediocre, and ideas everyone opposed in planning often turn out fun once built.
principles.how: When the team is split, have the director make the call and explain the reasoning; build promising unpopular ideas and judge them in the game.
principles.anti_pattern: Settling design direction by headcount.
principles.example: Metal Gear Solid 3 — the wound treatment system had only four supporters at first
principles.quote: Ideas decided by majority end up being the safest ideas. In other words, the most mediocre.

principles.principle: Share every problem and possible solution with the decision-maker
principles.why: Whoever holds the power must stay balanced and well informed; without transparency anyone can make the wrong call, and without reasoning direction turns into dictatorship.
principles.how: Before major decisions, ask the team to lay out the problems and candidate solutions they see, then decide with that information.
principles.anti_pattern: A leader barking irrational orders with paper-thin reasoning.
principles.quote: Anyone could make the wrong call when faced with a lack of transparency.

principles.principle: Brighten character extremities so their movement reads clearly
principles.why: Sakurai overrode the chosen Mii maid outfit to make the socks white, because brighter extremities make it easier to see a character's movement.
principles.how: Color hands, feet or socks in brighter values than the body so limb motion stands out.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. — Mii Fighter maid outfit with white socks
principles.quote: That's because brighter extremities make it easier to see a character's movement.

summary: Build risk into the inputs themselves, so the most powerful option requires passing through the most vulnerable positions, then scale the reward to that risk, and decide on purpose how much execution difficulty your audience can handle.
takeaways: The shoryuken input passes through the most dangerous stick positions
Reversals should be strongest when the opponent is closest
A high-risk move should deliver a big reward
Reward full command inputs without making them mandatory

principles.principle: Route your strongest reversal's input through the most vulnerable positions
principles.why: The shoryuken's forward, down, down-forward command steps toward the opponent, drops guard against aerial attacks, then reaches the most dangerous stick position, so pulling it off turns vulnerability into an anti-air.
principles.how: Design special-move inputs so that starting the input leaves the player exposed, making each attempt a gamble.
principles.example: Street Fighter II — the shoryuken command
principles.quote: In other words, this is the most dangerous stick position possible.

principles.principle: Make reversal moves strongest when the opponent is closest
principles.why: SFII's shoryuken is more powerful at its base and invincible at the start, so it is most effective the closer the opponent comes, exactly when you are most at risk of counterattack.
principles.how: Give anti-air or reversal moves startup invincibility and peak damage at close range, and tune them alongside input difficulty, input time, opponent speed and miss punishment.
principles.example: Street Fighter II — shoryuken strongest near its base, invincible at startup
principles.quote: The closer they get, the greater the potential to turn things around— a perfect example of risk and reward philosophy.

principles.principle: Scale each move's reward to the risk of using it
principles.why: Sakurai feels SFII's heavy shoryuken, the riskiest variant, could have been even stronger, because a move with high risk should deliver a big reward.
principles.how: When moves come in light, medium and heavy versions, make the riskiest one's payoff clearly the largest.
principles.anti_pattern: Underpaying the riskiest option.
principles.example: Street Fighter II — light, medium and heavy shoryuken
principles.quote: A move with high risk should deliver a big reward.

principles.principle: Reward full command inputs, but never make them mandatory in casual games
principles.why: Ryu's full-command shoryuken in Smash is stronger with more invincibility, but making it essential would have split players who can and can't execute it, so it stayed casual-friendly.
principles.how: Offer a one-button version of special moves and give the full command a modest bonus such as extra damage or invincibility frames.
principles.anti_pattern: Balancing so a hard input is required to compete.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. — Ryu's one-button vs. command shoryuken
principles.quote: For the sake of keeping things casual, we went ahead with the current balance.

summary: Pick the bold concept that your current production situation uniquely makes possible (Ultimate's "Everyone is here!" was only viable because the team and toolset carried over), then plan exhaustively, rebuild the fundamentals for the new feel, and design within hard limits on labor, storage and secrecy.
takeaways: A retained team and toolset made 'Everyone is here!' feasible
Finish the next proposal before the current project ends
Plan 70–100 changes per fighter across every discipline
A tempo change means retuning every parameter from scratch
Spirits replaced costly solo content by reusing borrowed characters
games: Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS / Wii U

principles.principle: Pick the bold concept your production continuity makes uniquely affordable
principles.why: Earlier Smash games rebuilt everything with new teams, but Ultimate kept Bandai Namco's team and dev environment on similar hardware, so bringing back every fighter became feasible; Sakurai saw it as the one chance to do it.
principles.how: Before choosing a sequel's headline concept, take stock of what carries over (team, tools, assets, hardware architecture) and aim at what that makes possible.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — 'Everyone is here!'
principles.quote: I knew if there would ever be a chance to include everyone, this would be it!

principles.principle: Have the next proposal ready before the current project wraps
principles.why: Sakurai finished Ultimate's 200-plus-page proposal the same day as Smash for's final video presentation, because staying ahead was the only way to keep the dev team together.
principles.how: Draft the follow-up proposal, with feature lists and per-character adjustments, during the tail end of the current project.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — proposal finished the same day Smash for's final presentation aired
principles.quote: I had to stay ahead if I wanted to keep the dev team together.

principles.principle: Retune every gameplay parameter whenever you change the game's tempo
principles.why: Ultimate raised the tempo over Smash for (but kept it below Melee), and even jumps and knockback were sped up, which meant none of Smash for's parameters could be reused.
principles.how: When changing game speed, plan time to rebuild all movement and combat values instead of porting old ones.
principles.anti_pattern: Carrying old tuning values into a faster game.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — tempo between Melee and Smash for
principles.quote: It may sound simple, but increasing the game's tempo meant we couldn't reuse any of the parameters from Smash Bros. for.

principles.principle: Build solo modes from your game's existing strengths when budgets are tight
principles.why: A Subspace Emissary-style mode and Trophies were too costly at Ultimate's scale, so Spirits reused Smash's borrowed characters, worlds and sounds to recreate situations, with World of Light tying the battles together.
principles.how: Design solo content around assets you already have; let players over-power themselves as a chosen difficulty, but give fewer rewards when they do.
principles.anti_pattern: Solo content that's just one versus battle after another.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — Spirits and World of Light
principles.quote: If you're too overpowered, though, you won't receive as many rewards.

summary: When you pitch or present a new game, don't define it by comparison to existing titles. Explain what makes it its own thing and let listeners make comparisons on their own.
takeaways: People need references, but don't invite comparisons yourself
A truly analogous game makes people just play the original
Only sequels should sell themselves by pointing to other games
References mean different things to different generations

principles.principle: Pitch your game on its own terms, not as a copy of another
principles.why: If your game is that analogous to another title, people may just play the original, and a company should avoid copycat accusations; only sequels should point to other games as selling points.
principles.how: Open your proposal by describing your game's own core experience without naming another game; let listeners make comparisons themselves.
principles.anti_pattern: Selling a new game as 'X, but with Y'.
principles.quote: In your proposal and your final product, do your best to let things shine in a way all their own.

principles.principle: Check that your audience shares a reference before using it
principles.why: Comparisons mean different things depending on generation and experience; 'Mario' can mean the NES game, Mario Odyssey or just the character.
principles.how: Use comparisons only when the situation and listener make them helpful, and never measure by your own play history alone.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming your own gaming history is everyone's reference point.
principles.example: 'Mario' — Super Mario Bros. on the NES vs. Mario Odyssey vs. the character
principles.quote: Every generation has different knowledge and different sensibilities, so it's best not to measure things based on your own personal experiences.

summary: If you make games at a company, understand the trade you made (steady pay and shared risk, in exchange for not personally profiting from hits) and choose to support your colleagues instead of feeling forced into it.
takeaways: Company work trades hit-driven upside for steady, shared-risk pay
Poor sales are never one person's fault
Companies provide far more than development itself
You chose this path; cooperate rather than feel forced

principles.principle: Treat cooperation at work as a choice you made, not a burden
principles.why: Friction between positions is inevitable, but company work is about supporting and being supported; it's the path you chose, so cooperating serves everyone better than feeling forced.
principles.how: When friction arises between roles, ask what you can do to help the other side do their best, and act on it.
principles.anti_pattern: Thinking you're being forced into your job.
principles.quote: Everyone at a company is in the same boat. Work together, and do what you can to bring out the best in each other.

principles.principle: Don't blame a single person for a game's poor sales
principles.why: Visuals, title, advertising, competing titles, market timing and platform all play a part, so poor sales can't truly be any one person's fault.
principles.how: In a post-release review, look across the whole chain from visuals and title to timing and platform before drawing conclusions.
principles.anti_pattern: Pinning a flop on one person.
principles.quote: No single person was responsible for making and selling the game, so poor sales can't be pinned on any one person.

principles.principle: Follow the partner company's rules when you work within it
principles.why: Sakurai is a freelancer, yet because much of his work involves cooperating with other companies, he does what's expected and always abides by their rules.
principles.how: When joining or contracting with a studio, learn its rules and processes and follow them.
principles.example: Sakurai's own freelance work with partner companies
principles.quote: Still, much of the work I do involves cooperating with other companies, so I do what's expected of me and always abide by their rules.

summary: If players will share your movies online anyway, make showcase videos that aren't tied to game progress, produce them like film (plot, storyboards, animatics, then final CG and sound), and push every shot bolder than "good enough".
takeaways: Movies used as progression rewards get posted online anyway
Make showcase videos not tied to progress, for everyone
Plot, storyboards and animatics set structure before CG
Capture gameplay footage with debug and replay tools
When it's good enough, zoom in and go bolder
games: Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS / Wii U

principles.principle: Don't make shareable movies the reward for game progress
principles.why: Brawl's per-fighter movies were meant to reward progress in Subspace Emissary, but people posted them online before release, so they stopped being much of a reward.
principles.how: Assume in-game movies will be uploaded at launch; use them as marketing everyone can watch rather than as progression payoffs.
principles.anti_pattern: Spending heavily on in-game movies as unlock rewards.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Brawl — Subspace Emissary movies leaked via pre-release copies
principles.quote: This meant they really weren't much of a reward.

principles.principle: Lock a trailer's structure and length with animatics before CG production
principles.why: Fighter reveals move from Sakurai's plot (cuts, character behavior, music cues) to storyboards to animatics, at which point the video's structure and length are essentially set before CG production begins.
principles.how: Write a cut-by-cut plot, storyboard it, then make an animatic by moving and stretching storyboard art and approve its timing before any final rendering.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. — fighter reveal production pipeline
principles.quote: At this point, the video's structure and length are essentially set.

principles.principle: Capture trailer gameplay with replay and debug camera tools
principles.why: Smash's gameplay segments are recorded by dev team members using debug and replay features to find the best camera angles, then repeatedly checked and restructured.
principles.how: Build replay playback with a free debug camera so trailer shots can be re-framed and re-shot from recorded matches.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. — fighter reveal gameplay segments
principles.quote: They capture footage using debug and replay features to find the best camera angles.

principles.principle: When a shot feels good enough, zoom in and go bolder
principles.why: Sakurai's most frequent notes on reveal footage were to push past 'good enough': bolder framing, a changed angle of view, more interaction between fighters, a balance of serious and comical, and syncing to music.
principles.how: Run each trailer shot through those checks: zoom in, change the angle of view, add interactions, balance serious and comic beats, cut to the music.
principles.anti_pattern: Settling for safe, adequate framing.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. — fighter reveal gameplay segments
principles.quote: When you think something's good enough, zoom in and go bolder.

summary: Use a sequel's head start (an existing system and tools) to expand the game, but make it clearly more fun and impactful than the one before, because a sequel that just repeats the original can expect about half the sales.
takeaways: Making the same thing again roughly halves sales
A sequel's existing system gives a big head start
Sequel sales depend on how good the first game was
Convince players it's more fun and impactful than before
games: Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS / Wii U

principles.principle: Spend a sequel's head start on expanding the system or the content
principles.why: Games need an underlying system, structure and tools before content can be made, so a sequel can improve that system and either expand it or get a large head start on content.
principles.how: At sequel kickoff, list what the existing system and tools give you and decide explicitly whether the saved effort goes to system expansion or more content.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. for 3DS/Wii U to Ultimate — same team, similar dev environment
principles.quote: Hence, by developing a sequel, you can improve on the existing system— and either focus on expanding it, or get a large head-start on the actual content.

principles.principle: Make the sequel clearly more fun and impactful than its predecessor
principles.why: Making the same thing again roughly halves sales, and fans who see the same scale and similar content may feel they've already experienced it.
principles.how: Write down how the sequel is more fun and more impactful than the last game, and make sure scale, content and the reveal show it.
principles.anti_pattern: Remaking the same game at the same scale.
principles.quote: But above all, the most vital thing is convincing players that it's more fun and impactful than its predecessor.

principles.principle: Give every assignment your best, sequel or original
principles.why: Sakurai sees meaning and value in both sequels and new titles; which he makes depends on who offers the work, and a sequel won't sell if it isn't well made.
principles.how: Treat a sequel assignment with the same full effort as an original, because the quality of each entry drives sales of the next.
principles.anti_pattern: Coasting on a series' name.
principles.quote: What matters most is that I carry out my assignments to the best of my ability.

summary: Supervise by showing, not telling: give concrete visual feedback (retouched images, diagrams, side-by-sides with the source) on everything players will see, with special attention to readability, collision matching animation, and staying true to the original's feel.
takeaways: Show visual feedback with retouched images instead of text
Fix both collision and animation when hits look wrong
Keep fighters and platforms readable in dark scenes
Honor the source's feeling rather than copying it
Scrutinize every stage detail from a top-down view

principles.principle: Show visual feedback with retouched images instead of describing it
principles.why: Remote supervision runs mostly on text, but showing communicates more clearly than telling, so Sakurai retouches or draws art himself to explain each request.
principles.how: Attach a paintover, retouched screenshot or diagram next to the original for every visual note, with one line on what to change.
principles.anti_pattern: Text-only feedback on a visual problem.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — retouches for Steve, Pyra/Mythra, Kazuya and event banners
principles.quote: but since showing tends to communicate more clearly than telling, I sometimes retouch or draw art myself to explain what I mean.

principles.principle: Make collision and animation agree so hits look and feel right
principles.why: Attacks that look like they should hit but don't, or that keep hitting after the swing, feel wrong; Sakurai fixes both collision and animation.
principles.how: When a hit feels off, adjust hitbox shape and timing together with the animation's arc or pose until the visual and the collision match.
principles.anti_pattern: Hit visuals and collision that disagree.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — Pyra's forward aerial collision shortened; Mythra's slash aligned to a diagonal
principles.quote: A common issue: attacks that look like they should hit, but don't.

principles.principle: Check that fighters and platforms stay readable in dark or busy scenes
principles.why: Players must see what matters: Sakurai flagged a block hidden by vignetting, fighters lost in Mishima Dojo's shadows (clearer in a desaturated image), hard-to-see platforms and a too-dark costume.
principles.how: Desaturate screenshots to check value contrast, and relight or recolor any character, platform or costume that disappears.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting key objects blend into dark backgrounds.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — Mishima Dojo shadows, Castlevania vignetting, Enderman costume
principles.quote: In Mishima Dojo, fighters in shadow became difficult to see.

principles.principle: Honor the source's feeling rather than copying it literally
principles.why: Sakurai compares against the original game when making requests, but the goal is to honor its feeling and do what works best, not to match it directly.
principles.how: Put the source's art or screenshots beside yours and match its palette, saturation and signature poses where they serve the feel.
principles.anti_pattern: Copying source material literally.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — Kazuya's knockdown pose and Final Smash; CG movie shots pushed toward FFVII: Advent Children
principles.quote: I don't want us to just copy the originals, but honor the feeling and do what works best.

summary: When faces are small or stylized, push expressions past the point where they feel finished, because CG loses information and "too much is about right", while shaping them to the character's anatomy and source material.
takeaways: Small CG faces need bigger expressions than feel natural
When it feels done, push the movement a step further
Show eye whites top and bottom; offset the teeth
Respect the source: Steve only blinks, so bodies emote

principles.principle: Push facial expressions past 'done', because CG loses information
principles.why: Smash faces are small and need no lip sync, yet most incoming artwork had expression shifts that were too small; since CG loses information, too much is about right for realistic and cartoony styles alike.
principles.how: Once an expression looks finished, exaggerate it one more step and judge it in-game at real viewing size.
principles.anti_pattern: Subtle expressions on characters seen at small sizes.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — Wolf's damage face retouch
principles.quote: Get it to where it feels done, then go a step further and make the movements even bigger.

principles.principle: Build expressions on anatomy: eye whites, offset teeth, jaw structure
principles.why: Sakurai's details include visible eye whites above and below on wide-open eyes and teeth that aren't directly aligned; Wolf's damage face was emphasized to suit a wolf's jaw.
principles.how: For shocked faces show eye white above and below the iris, offset upper and lower teeth, and size mouth shapes to the character's jaw.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — Wolf's damage face
principles.quote: Making the whites of wide-open eyes visible at both the top and the bottom or making sure the upper and lower teeth aren't directly aligned

principles.principle: When the source has no facial range, express emotion through movement
principles.why: Steve's only facial animation is a blink, so his other movements must make up for it; putting the source material first matters more than adding faces.
principles.how: Keep faithful but limited faces as they are and give those characters more expressive body motion instead.
principles.anti_pattern: Inventing facial expressions the source character never had.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — Steve only blinks
principles.quote: We do have to make up for that with his other movements, but that's all part of putting the source material first.

summary: Shape impact sounds for busy action: reach a strong level almost instantly and keep the reverb tail short, so every hit registers right away and doesn't bury the next one.
takeaways: Impact sounds must reach a strong level almost immediately
Short reverb keeps overlapping hits from becoming noise
Trim rapid-jab sounds to just feel like consecutive hits
A heavy hit's sound should finish during hitstop

principles.principle: Make impact sounds reach a strong level almost immediately
principles.why: An impact sound must never feel late, because players need a reaction to their attack right away; it can't literally start at peak volume, but must get to a strong sound almost immediately.
principles.how: Shorten the attack of hit sounds so they peak at the very beginning.
principles.anti_pattern: Hit sounds that swell in slowly and feel late.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. — impact sound revisions
principles.quote: It's vital that players get a reaction to their attack right away.

principles.principle: Keep reverb tails short so overlapping hits stay distinct
principles.why: With four to eight players, sounds overlap constantly; long echoes feel strong but get lost and bury the next sound in noise, so rapid jabs are trimmed to just feel like consecutive hits.
principles.how: Trim reverb on impact sounds in busy scenes and cut multi-hit sounds to the shortest length that still reads as separate hits.
principles.anti_pattern: Long, echoing tails that sound great alone but muddy the mix.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. — rapid jab sounds pared down
principles.quote: Next, don't drag out the reverberation too much.

principles.principle: Finish a heavy hit's sound during hitstop, before action resumes
principles.why: Strong attacks freeze the screen for hitstop while the sound keeps playing; ideally the main part of the sound is over before the action resumes.
principles.how: Time heavy-hit sounds so their main body plays out within the hitstop freeze.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. — strong attacks with hitstop
principles.quote: The sound keeps playing in the meantime, but ideally the main part of the sound effect should be over before the action resumes.

principles.principle: Choose sounds that serve your game, not just sounds that are good
principles.why: 'Strong attack, light reverb' fits Smash's crowded, fast battles; the right choice depends on the game, so the goal is the type of sound that best serves it.
principles.how: Judge sound effects in the game's real worst-case context rather than in isolation.
principles.anti_pattern: Picking sounds because they sound good on their own.
principles.quote: it's not just about creating "good" sounds— it's also about finding the right type of sounds to best serve your game.

summary: When you adapt a classic character, work from the original production material (for Mr. Game & Watch, the actual LCD patterns Nintendo provided), because the original designers' ingenuity is worth studying firsthand.
takeaways: Nintendo gave the Smash team original Game & Watch LCD patterns
Original patterns show the era's unique ingenuity

principles.principle: Work from original source material when adapting a classic character
principles.why: During Smash development the team was given the original Game & Watch LCD patterns as reference, material Sakurai calls precious and a testament to the era's ingenuity.
principles.how: Obtain the original sprites, LCD patterns or model sheets from the rightsholder and use them as your primary reference.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. — Game & Watch LCD patterns used as reference
principles.quote: During Smash Bros. development, we were given some truly precious LCD patterns as reference.

summary: Make choosing fast: question the input devices and menu conventions everyone takes for granted, and treat every new device as a chance to speed up selection, without burying beginners under expert-only shortcuts.
takeaways: Menu selection is the input that most needs to be fast
Sakurai wanted a clicky scroll wheel on controllers since GameCube
D-pads beat repeated analog-stick taps for menus
Advanced shortcuts can narrow a UI's appeal to beginners

principles.principle: Make menu selection fast; cut the steps to the player's choice
principles.why: Of all game inputs, menu selection is what Sakurai most wants to be quick; a scroll wheel would let him zip right to his choice instead of tapping repeatedly.
principles.how: Count inputs to the most common menu choices and reduce them; support D-pad navigation rather than repeated stick taps.
principles.anti_pattern: Menus that require tap-tap-tapping the analog stick.
principles.example: Nintendo GameCube / Smash Bros. Melee — scroll wheel suggestion
principles.quote: A scroll wheel would let me zip right to my choice and be done in a flash.

principles.principle: Give menu navigation a clicky, tactile step
principles.why: Games are about play, so tactile 'clicky' feedback, like a notched wheel or a D-pad, makes even selection feel more immersive.
principles.how: Make each step of menu movement distinct and crisp so scrolling feels physical.
principles.example: D-pad vs. analog stick in menus
principles.quote: Games are about play, so that tactile feedback would make gameplay feel more immersive.

principles.principle: Treat every new input device as a chance to improve UI
principles.why: Sakurai re-examines things taken for granted and has approached new devices as UI opportunities ever since designing Melee.
principles.how: When a platform adds an input such as a wheel, touch or gyro, prototype using it to speed up selection.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Melee era hardware suggestions
principles.quote: But new devices are new opportunities!

principles.principle: Layer shortcuts over a beginner-friendly path; don't depend on them
principles.why: The more advanced the shortcut options, the less inexperienced players use them, and the UI can lose broad appeal, so it's a tough line to walk.
principles.how: Keep a simple default way through every menu and add shortcuts as optional accelerators for experienced players.
principles.anti_pattern: Expert-only shortcut systems as the main way to navigate.
principles.quote: Still, the more advanced your shortcut options, the less inexperienced players will use them, and you may end up with a UI that lacks broad appeal

summary: Use rankings to give players purpose and fair matches, but present standing so that most players feel successful (a score where higher is better, measured against the whole player base, with the top player hidden) instead of a raw leaderboard that tells nearly everyone they're losing.
takeaways: Leaderboards give purpose by linking effort to higher goals
Raw ranks make almost everyone feel like they're losing
GSP ranks against total players, so higher is better
Hide the top player; filter cheats; separate elite players
Matchmaking range must balance finding matches against fairness

principles.principle: Link ranked results to an incentive to aim higher
principles.why: Without a leaderboard you're just fighting and there's little thrill; it's vital that the result of hard work connects to a reason to push further.
principles.how: Give competitive modes a visible standing that moves with performance so players have something to climb.
principles.quote: It's vital that the result of your hard work is linked to an incentive to aim even higher.

principles.principle: Express rank so improvement raises the number, not a position
principles.why: Ordinary leaderboards tell anyone below first that they're losing, and 400th or x-millionth place saps motivation; GSP measures power against the global player count, so higher is better.
principles.how: Show standing as how many players someone is above, computed against total population, instead of a position where lower is better.
principles.anti_pattern: Raw position leaderboards for huge player bases.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — Global Smash Power (GSP)
principles.quote: In other words, unlike a leaderboard where the lower number is better, this system says that the higher number is better.

principles.principle: Hide the top player and wall off the elite in their own tier
principles.why: Seeing how far you are from the world's best makes people give up, and the info only matters to the very elite; Elite Smash gives top players status and keeps them from matching lower-ranked players.
principles.how: Don't surface the #1 player's identity or score to general players; create an elite tier that matches top players with each other.
principles.anti_pattern: Showing everyone their distance from the top.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — GSP obscures the top player; Elite Smash
principles.quote: Players will just see how far away they are and want to give up.

principles.principle: Balance matchmaking range between finding matches and fair skill gaps
principles.why: Players need opponents of similar skill who are also nearby and online at the same time, which is rare in low-population areas; too narrow means no match, too broad means mismatches.
principles.how: Tune the skill range by region and time of day, widening it only as far as needed for players to find matches.
principles.anti_pattern: A fixed range that is either too narrow or too broad.
principles.quote: If the matching range is too narrow, players will never find a match, but if it's too broad, players will match with people far outside their skill level.

summary: Motivate yourself by imagining something closing in on you. Treat a deadline as a pursuer to outrun rather than a goal you'll reach eventually, without actually leaving the work until the last day.
takeaways: Imagining a pursuer took Sakurai from last to first
Give yourself something to run from, not just a goal
Tell yourself you only have a few hours left
Don't literally wait for the last day to start

principles.principle: Give yourself something to run from, not just a goal to reach
principles.why: Sakurai went from last to first in foot races by imagining a three-meter machine chasing him; a deadline or endpoint closing in can be surprisingly effective motivation.
principles.how: Frame upcoming milestones as something approaching that you must get ahead of.
principles.anti_pattern: Running as if chasing your own shadow.
principles.example: Sakurai's middle-school foot races
principles.quote: instead of setting a target or a destination you're heading toward, give yourself something to run from.

principles.principle: Tell yourself a task has only a few hours left
principles.why: Thinking you can finish whenever lets work drift, while believing time is short gets things done; but it doesn't mean actually waiting for the last day.
principles.how: Set a short, self-imposed time limit before starting each task, well ahead of the real deadline.
principles.anti_pattern: Leaving work until the real last day, like summer homework.
principles.quote: I believe you'll really get things done if you tell yourself you only have a few hours left.
